summary: Build durable, precise command of ecology role vocabulary (producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer) for 8–10s by binding each word to its FUNCTION in the flow of food rather than to a fixed list of example animals. The central discriminations are producer vs consumer (makes its own food vs eats others), predator vs prey as RELATIONAL roles (the same animal can be both depending on the pairing), and decomposer as a distinct, frequently-forgotten role that returns nutrients to the soil. Work across a labelled habitat scene (anchoring words to visible organisms), active sorting for retrieval, and spoken use-in-context to reveal whether the learner truly owns the relational and recycling meanings.
misconceptions: Thinking 'producer' means a factory/maker in the human sense, or that producers are 'the strong ones', rather than organisms that make their own food from sunlight.
Treating predator and prey as fixed identities — not realising the same animal is prey to one organism and predator to another.
Forgetting decomposers entirely, or thinking dead things just disappear rather than being broken down and recycled.
Confusing consumer and predator — assuming any animal that eats is a 'predator', missing that herbivores are consumers but not predators.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal role glossary over one habitat scene
steps: Study a single rich woodland scene with named organisms (oak and grass, rabbit, mouse, fox, owl, beetle, fungi on a dead log).

Tap/point to each organism and reveal its role bound to its function: oak and grass = 'PRODUCER — makes its own food from sunlight'; rabbit = 'CONSUMER — eats plants; here it is PREY to the fox'; fox = 'PREDATOR — hunts the rabbit'; fungi = 'DECOMPOSER — breaks down the dead and returns nutrients to the soil'.

Tap the mouse and see it flagged BOTH as PREY (to the owl above) AND PREDATOR (to the beetle below); note it is also shown feeding on grass seeds, so it eats both plants and animals. Answer a lift-the-flap question 'so is the mouse a predator or prey?' and then check it against 'both — it depends who you compare it to'.
Drill into the fungi close-up to see nutrients returning to the soil, so the decomposer role is understood as recycling, not just 'eating dead things'.
activities.insight: The five core role words name precise functions in the flow of food, and predator/prey name a relationship rather than a fixed identity — the same organism can be predator in one pairing and prey in another.

activities.title: Sort organisms into roles, then flip the pairing
steps: Drag or place each organism into role bins: producer | consumer | decomposer.
Within a shown pairing, assign predator and prey (e.g. fox–rabbit, owl–mouse).
Take a 'flip the pairing' twist: when the mouse's partner changes from the owl to the beetle, reclassify it from prey to predator, and explain why.

Sort consumers into sub-kinds — herbivore, carnivore, omnivore — using a correct example for each where the scene supports it (rabbit = herbivore; owl = carnivore; the mouse, which the scene shows eating both the beetle and grass seeds, = omnivore). The fox is shown only eating meat here, but real foxes also eat fruit and berries, so they are usually called omnivores. Do not mark 'carnivore' as the only right answer for the fox.
activities.insight: Retrieval sorting is intended to move the words from recognition to recall, and reclassifying the same animal when its partner changes makes the relational nature of predator/prey concrete; herbivore/carnivore/omnivore are sub-kinds of consumer.

activities.title: Talk me through who's who — spoken use in context
steps: Face a woodland scene: oak trees, caterpillars, blue tits, a sparrowhawk, fungi on a dead log.
Talk through who's who and what happens to energy and to the dead wood, using whichever words fit: producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer.

Answer probing questions: 'You called the blue tit a predator — is it also prey to anything in this wood?'; 'What does the fungus do that an ordinary consumer does not?'; 'Which animal here could be an omnivore, and why?'; 'Which organism is the producer, and what earns it that name?'
Transfer the vocabulary to a fresh organism not yet discussed.
activities.insight: Correct USE in context (not recited definitions) reveals whether the learner holds predator/prey as relational, keeps decomposer distinct from consumer, and distinguishes herbivore/carnivore/omnivore.

checkQuestion: Present a woodland scene: oak trees, caterpillars, blue tits, a sparrowhawk, and fungi growing on a dead log. Say: 'Talk me through who's who here, and what happens to energy and to the dead wood — use whichever of these words fit: producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer.' Listen for correct use, not recited definitions.
checkAnswer: Uses the terms accurately in context: oak = producer; caterpillar = primary consumer / herbivore and prey; blue tit = consumer / predator of caterpillars and prey to the sparrowhawk; sparrowhawk = predator / carnivore; fungi = decomposer breaking down the dead log and recycling nutrients back to the soil. Relational terms (predator/prey) are attached to the right pairs, and the decomposer's recycling role is stated.
